title: Can a non-Muslim visit a Muslim grave?
headline: Maliki and Hanbali texts allow a non-Muslim to visit a Muslim grave; most fatwas address the reverse case

summary.text: The Maliki jurist Hattab permits a non-Muslim to visit a Muslim grave, advising supplication to God rather than for the deceased and modest dress, and the Hanbali al-Insaf says a non-Muslim should not be prevented from visiting his Muslim father's grave. Most of the fiqh and fatwa material addresses a Muslim visiting a non-Muslim grave: the Shafi'i school permits it, and recent fatwas permit it for reflection and a lesson, without supplication for the deceased. The ruling turns on distinguishing the visit itself from the funeral prayer and seeking forgiveness, which Quran 9:84 and the hadith restrict.

paragraphs.text: Quran 9:84 forbids the funeral prayer over the hypocrites and standing at their graves. Ibn Baz reads it as a prohibition on the funeral prayer over hypocrites and on standing at their graves to supplicate for them, while at a Muslim's grave one stands and asks forgiveness and steadfastness for him. Dar al-Ifta al-Misriyyah, citing Kashshaf al-Qina', reports that most exegetes take "stand at his grave" to mean standing for supplication and seeking forgiveness. On that reading the verse restricts two acts, the funeral prayer and intercession at the grave, not mere presence at a grave.

Quran 9:113 states that it is not for the Prophet and the believers to ask forgiveness for the polytheists, even near of kin, once it is clear they are companions of the Fire. Quran 9:114 explains that Ibrahim's seeking forgiveness for his father was only because of a promise, after which he disassociated himself from him. Quran 9:80 addresses the same point with the "seventy times" image.

IslamOnline invokes Quran 17:70, "Surely We have honored the children of Adam," as general enough to cover Muslims and non-Muslims, so that graves of either are treated with respect. Qays ibn Sa'd and Sahl ibn Hunayf stood at al-Qadisiyya for a funeral and, told the deceased was a protected non-Muslim, cited the Prophet's standing and his words "Is it not a soul?".

Abu Hurayra reports that the Prophet visited his mother's grave and wept, and said: "I asked my Lord for permission to seek forgiveness for her, but I was not given permission. And I asked Him for permission to visit her grave, and I was given permission. So visit the graves, for they remind you of death". It is graded Sahih in Sahih Muslim, and the same narration in Sunan an-Nasa'i carries the gradings Sahih (Abu Ghuddah), Sahih (Al-Albani) and Sahih Muslim (Zubair Ali Zai). The wording "I used to forbid you to visit graves, but now visit them" is graded Sahih (Darussalam) at Sunan an-Nasa'i 5652 and Sahih (Al-Albani) at Sunan Abi Dawud 3235; the Nasa'i 2033 version adds "let whoever wishes to visit do so, but do not utter anything unsuitable," graded Sahih (Darussalam).

On standing for a non-Muslim funeral, al-Bukhari 1311, where the Prophet says "Whenever you see a funeral, stand up," is Sahih, and Muslim 960c, that he and his Companions stood for a Jew's bier until it was out of sight, is Sahih. Abu Dawud 3174, "Death is a terrifying thing, so when you see a funeral, stand up," is Sahih across three graders, and Nasa'i 1922, on a Jewish woman's funeral, is Sahih. A conflicting report, Nasa'i 1929, has him say "We only stood up for the angels," graded Sahih isnad by Abu Ghuddah and Al-Albani but da'if by Zubair Ali Zai. Ali's burial of Abu Talib at the Prophet's instruction, "Go and bury him," is Sahih.

The Maliki jurist Hattab, in Mawahib al-Jalil as cited by SeekersGuidance, addresses a non-Muslim visiting a Muslim grave and calls it "perfectly fine," with no prayer for the deceased but supplication to God and modest dress. The Hanbali al-Mardawi, in al-Insaf as cited by Islamweb and Dar al-Ifta, says a non-Muslim should not be prevented from visiting his Muslim father's grave, and that visiting a non-Muslim's grave is permitted. The Hanafi Ibn Abidin, in Radd al-Muhtar, addresses a non-Muslim entering the grave pit of his Muslim relative to bury him and calls it disliked (makruh).

The Shafi'i al-Sharwani, on Tuhfat al-Muhtaj quoting al-'Ubab and al-Majmu', permits a Muslim visiting a non-Muslim's grave (mubah), the position of most and approved in al-Majmu', with no distinction between relative and stranger. Al-Mawardi alone asserted it is haram. The Hanbali Kashshaf al-Qina' states that visiting a non-Muslim's grave is permitted and that standing at his grave is like visiting it.

The apparent conflict between Quran 9:84, which forbids standing at the grave of a disbeliever, and the Prophet's visit to his mother's grave is reconciled by saying the verse targets the funeral prayer and supplication for the deceased, while the hadith itself separates the two permissions, granting the visit and refusing the seeking of forgiveness. Ibn Baz draws the same line: the verse bars praying over the hypocrite and standing at his grave, whereas at a Muslim's grave one stands and supplicates.

The conflict between the general command "visit the graves" and the ban on seeking forgiveness for one who died outside Islam is resolved by Ibn Uthaymeen by tying the command to its stated reason, that graves remind one of death, which is present at every grave, while the ban attaches specifically to supplication for the deceased. The Permanent Committee makes the same split between the purpose of visiting a Muslim grave and the purpose of visiting a non-Muslim one.

Within the Shafi'i school, al-Mawardi's assertion of prohibition stands against the majority's permissibility, with al-Majmu' approving the latter and extending it to relatives and strangers alike. The Hanafi karaha on a non-Muslim entering his Muslim relative's grave is confined by the text to descending into the pit to bury, an act distinct from standing at the grave to visit. On standing at funerals, the Bukhari and Muslim reports command it, Nasa'i carries the "angels" explanation, and Ibn Uthaymeen reconciles them by saying the standing is a recommended practice and that the Prophet's later ceasing to stand was to show it is not obligatory.

The Permanent Committee (fatwa 15509) holds that visiting graves is prescribed in general: Muslim graves are visited to supplicate and seek forgiveness for them and to take a lesson, while non-Muslim graves are visited for a lesson and a warning. Ibn Baz permits visiting a disbeliever's grave for the sake of taking a lesson, citing the Prophet's visit to his mother's grave and his being granted only the visit, not the seeking of forgiveness. Ibn Uthaymeen holds visiting permissible in general, even the graves of disbelievers, because the reason given in the text, remembrance of death and the Hereafter, exists in all of them.

IslamQA (11890) permits visiting a non-Muslim's grave for a lesson only, and adds that the visitor should not greet him with salaam or supplicate for him. Sheikh Ahmad Kutty frames the purpose as reflection on one's own destiny and a strengthening of faith, and IslamOnline permits it for reflection while insisting on respect for non-Muslim graves. SeekersGuidance answers the exact question posed here in the affirmative, and Islamweb allows a non-Muslim woman to enter a Muslim cemetery to attend a relative's burial, provided nothing objectionable such as free mixing or loud wailing occurs.

On funerals rather than graves, Dar al-Ifta al-Misriyyah permits a Muslim to follow a non-Muslim relative's funeral as a form of kindness and maintaining ties, Mathabah holds there is no objection in principle with the same conditions, and Darul Iftaa Chicago permits condolence visits while saying Muslims do not attend the religious ceremony. Against these, Muftionline cites Quran 9:84 to say attending a non-Muslim funeral is not permissible, and Ibn Taymiyya and Ibn Uthaymeen distinguish visiting a sick non-Muslim, which is fine, from following his funeral, which they disallow. What a non-Muslim visitor does at the grave is described in one source: do not pray for the deceased, call upon God Himself, dress modestly, and the general etiquette of the graveyard applies, since it is impermissible to walk on Muslim graves, sit on them or step on them.
